findings.statement: The continuous recording of employees' application use, websites visited and working time, and the individual productivity scores generated from it, are personal data of identified employees processed by automated means, so the GDPR applies to the monitoring and scoring.
The company must establish a lawful basis under Article 6(1) for the continuous recording and the generation of the productivity scores before carrying out that processing.
Employee consent is unlikely to constitute a valid lawful basis because of the clear imbalance of power between the employer and its employees.

Because the processing takes place in the employment context and involves employee monitoring, the company must comply with the more specific rules and safeguards adopted under Article 88(1) in the applicable jurisdiction.

The company must specify the purposes of the monitoring and scoring and ensure the recorded data are adequate, relevant and limited to those purposes, applying purpose limitation and data minimisation.
The company must inform employees of the purposes of the monitoring and scoring, the retention period, their rights and the other core information at the time the data are collected.
Where records of websites visited reveal data on health, religion or other special categories, that data must not be processed unless a ground in Article 9(2) applies.

The company must ensure that performance evaluations based on the productivity score are not decisions based solely on automated processing producing legal effects or similarly significantly affecting employees, unless a ground in Article 22(2) applies.

The company must determine whether the monitoring and scoring are likely to result in a high risk to employees and, where they are, carry out a data protection impact assessment before the processing begins.

The system is an AI system intended to be used for monitoring and evaluating the performance of workers, an Annex III point 4(b) use case, and is therefore to be considered a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2).

The Article 6(3) exclusion from high-risk status is not available, because generating individual productivity scores evaluates employees' performance at work and therefore profiles natural persons within the meaning incorporated by Article 3(50), and profiling Annex III systems are always high-risk.

The company is a deployer of a high-risk AI system and must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, and must ensure effective human oversight by persons with the necessary competence, training and authority.
The company must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they are subject to the system's use at the workplace before putting the system into service there.

When employees are subject to decisions taken on the basis of the system's output, the company must inform them of that basis and provide meaningful information about the reasons, the categories of data and the right to contest.

Employees subject to score-based evaluations that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect them may request clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making, which the company as deployer must provide.

summaries.relevance: Brings the company's automated recording and scoring of employee activity within the GDPR, making data protection obligations the baseline of the whole answer.
Supplies the personal data definition under which the monitoring data and scores qualify as personal data of employees, the predicate for every GDPR obligation in the answer.
The source of the lawful-basis obligation that every element of the recording and scoring must satisfy before use.
Undermines consent as the available lawful basis given the imbalance of power between employer and employees in this scenario.
Points to the employment-specific safeguards that govern employee monitoring and that the company must additionally comply with.
Purpose limitation is the principle against which the breadth of continuous recording for productivity evaluation is measured here.
Data minimisation constrains the monitoring to what the productivity scoring actually requires.
Requires the company to give employees the core information about the monitoring and scoring at the point of collection.
Prohibits processing any captured browsing data that reveal special categories of data, a key risk in website monitoring of employees.
Sets the only escape grounds from the Article 9(1) prohibition for any special-category data the monitoring captures.
Limits decisions on employees' performance based solely on the automated score where those decisions have legal or similarly significant effects.
Sets the exceptions that would permit a solely automated score-based evaluation and so frames the manager's necessary role.
Requires the company to determine high-risk likelihood and, where found, run a DPIA before processing, the pre-deployment check for this monitoring.
Supplies the profiling definition the AI Act incorporates, allowing the productivity scoring to be recognised as profiling.
Lists monitoring and evaluating worker performance as a high-risk use case, matching the system's described use exactly.
Converts the Annex III employment use case into high-risk status, activating the deployer-obligation regime the answer relies on.
Is the hinge of the classification: it could exempt the system from high-risk status but not where it profiles employees.
Defines profiling by reference to the GDPR definition, which the individual productivity scoring meets.
Identifies the company as the deployer, attaching the Article 26 duties to it rather than to another actor.
Obliges the deployer to use the system per its instructions for use under appropriate measures, the primary operating constraint on the company.
Requires effective human oversight of the system's use, anchoring the role managers must play when relying on the scores.
Requires informing workers' representatives and affected workers before the system is put into service at the workplace, the AI Act's specific employee-monitoring duty.
Requires informing employees of decisions based on the system's output, with reasons, data categories and the right to contest, the duty that attaches directly to score-based evaluations.
Gives evaluated employees a right to an explanation of the AI system's role where the evaluation significantly affects them.

actions: Establish which Member State(s) govern the workforce so that the employment-context rules adopted under Article 88(1) GDPR applicable to this monitoring can be identified.
Confirm which Article 6(1) GDPR ground the company would rely on for the recording and the scoring, and whether any consent from employees could be valid given the imbalance described in Recital 43.
Determine whether the company also qualifies as a provider of the AI system, for example where it developed the software, as the findings above address the company's obligations as deployer only.
Verify against the system's actual design whether it performs profiling as incorporated by Article 3(50) of the AI Act and whether any Article 6(3) exclusion could still apply.
Establish whether the company is a financial entity to which DORA applies, since the scenario leaves its sector unstated and DORA was therefore not relied on.
